subject.title: Then
subject.author: Edwin Muir
subject.text:
There were no men and women then at all,
But the flesh lying alone,
And angry shadows fighting on a wall
Which now and then sent out a groan
Stifled in lime and stone,
And sweated now and then like tortured wood
Big drops that looked yet did not look like blood.

And yet as each drop came a shadow faded
And left the wall
There was a lull
Until another in its shadow arrayed it,
Came, fought and left a blood-mark on the wall.
And that was all; the blood was all.
If women had been there they might have wept
For the poor blood, unowned, unwanted,
Blank as forgotten script.
The wall was haunted
By mute maternal presences whose sighing
Fluttered the fighting shadows and shook the wall
As if that fury of death itself were dying.

title: The War Poem That Wouldn't Name the War
standfirst: In September 1940, Poetry magazine ran Edwin Muir's "Then" beside poems titled for refugees, for Wilfrid Owen, for the war itself. His poem names nobody — not the war, not a person, not even a man or a woman. A friend had already diagnosed exactly why, twenty-one years earlier.

sections.heading: Filed Between Two Poems That Name Names
sections.body:
"Then" reached readers on page 311 of Poetry magazine's September 1940 issue, a table of contents that reads like a roll call of the war Britain had just watched France lose: "Address to the Refugees," "Now That the War Is Here," "For Wilfrid Owen," "U.S. Writers in War." Immediately before Muir's poem sits [Children in San Diego](https://archive.org/details/sim_poetry_1940-09_56_6), by Millen Brand, subtitled "(Incident told by a friend)": stanzas about boys digging a trench on a Californian beach, playing at war in sight of real destroyers and periscopes near a naval base, until an actual rifle round finds one of them, Freddie, "trying to say" something with blood running over his lips while someone shouts "A twenty-two!" Brand names the boy, the beach, the base.

Muir names nothing. His poem opens by refusing even the minimal identification its own title promises: "There were no men and women then at all, / But the flesh lying alone." Whatever fight is underway on his wall belongs to no nation, no decade, not even a stated sex. Sandwiched between poems that spell out exactly who is fighting whom and where, "Then" reads like the one poem in its own war issue that has walked out of the war.

sections.heading: A Friend's Diagnosis, Twenty-One Years Early
sections.body:
Twenty-one years before "Then" appeared in print, a young writer named [John Ferrar Holms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ferrar_Holms) met Muir on a country walk outside Glasgow and went home to describe him, in [a letter to Hugh Kingsmill that Muir later reproduced in his own autobiography](https://gutenberg.ca/ebooks/muire-autobiography/muire-autobiography-00-e.html), with unnerving precision. It was the summer of 1919. Holms reported that Muir "far prefers the idea of Nietzsche's eternal return to the union which is at the heart of every mystic's vision" — a diagnosis of temperament, delivered after one afternoon's conversation about metaphysics with a man he had just met.

Read "Then" against that sentence and its shape stops looking accidental. Nothing in the poem moves forward. A shadow fights on the wall, sweats a blood-drop, and fades; "there was a lull"; another shadow "arrayed it" in the vacated space and fought in turn, leaving its own mark. Muir never lets the second combatant differ from the first, or the poem progress past the exchange: "And that was all; the blood was all." It is recurrence without variation or resolution — Nietzsche's wheel staged as a single unlit stretch of wall, with anonymous fighters taking turns to die on it. Holms had clocked the taste for that wheel in Muir a generation before Muir put it on the page.

sections.heading: The Death With No Enemy In It
sections.body:
"Then" did not stay a magazine poem. Three years later Muir carried it into [The Narrow Place](https://www.fadedpage.com/showbook.php?pid=20170426), the 1943 collection where it sits between "The River" and "The Refugees" — and where the whole book carries a dedication naming the same friend: "To J.F.H. (1897-1934)."

By then Holms had been dead for nine years, and not from any war. He broke his wrist [in a riding accident on Dartmoor with Peggy Guggenheim](https://spartacus-educational.com/SPholmsJ.htm); the operation to set it, on the morning of 19 January 1934, reportedly complicated by a heavy hangover, went wrong under the anaesthetic, and he died on the table. Muir, who called him ["the most remarkable man I ever met"](https://gutenberg.ca/ebooks/muire-autobiography/muire-autobiography-00-e.html) in the autobiography he was still drafting years afterward, never got to write him into a poem with an enemy in it, a war he could blame. The book "Then" belongs to is dedicated to a death that had no battle anywhere near it — a wrist, a doctor, a mistake. Set beside that fact, the poem's blood-soaked, nameless wall starts to look less like reportage on any real war than the only shape of violence Muir had to hand for a private loss: an old myth of anonymous combat, borrowed to carry a grief that had nothing to do with armies.

sections.heading: What Happened to Muir While the Poem Waited
sections.body:
Between the poem's two appearances, Muir's own life moved a long way toward the facelessness "Then" imagines. He and Willa were living in St Andrews when both failed to land teaching posts, and Muir joined the local Home Guard and took a clerk's job at [the Food Office in Dundee](https://gutenberg.ca/ebooks/muire-autobiography/muire-autobiography-00-e.html) — the desk where wartime Scotland's ration books were issued and stamped. His night duty there consisted of pacing alone around a telephone exchange from two until four in the morning, armed, he writes, with a shotgun that had no ammunition in it.

Then illness caught up with him. Overstraining himself carrying sandbags brought on chest pains bad enough that a local doctor warned he might not live another year without six weeks of complete rest. He had barely recovered when Willa was driven to a nursing home for what he calls, in the same account, "a difficult operation," and came back from the anaesthetic so weak that doctors kept her alive on sips of champagne while he sat beside her, by his own description, no longer able to reach her. She recovered so slowly that, he writes, years passed before she resembled what she had once been — years [one recent account of the marriage](https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v45/n18/robert-crawford/peerie-breeks) also describes simply as Edwin "depressed."

None of this is in "Then." But it falls in the three years between the poem's appearance in Poetry and its appearance in The Narrow Place, and it means the man revising his own war poem for book publication had, in the interval, become something close to the case his poem describes: not a poet with a name, just a body behind a ration-book counter, waiting through someone else's convalescence for a war that mostly reached him as blackout and rumour.

sections.heading: The Grief the Poem Won't Let Anyone Have
sections.body:
> If women had been there they might have wept
> For the poor blood, unowned, unwanted,
> Blank as forgotten script.
> The wall was haunted
> By mute maternal presences whose sighing
> Fluttered the fighting shadows and shook the wall
> As if that fury of death itself were dying.

Every verb in that closing image is hedged. The women are conditional — "if women had been there" — because the poem has already told us, in its first line, that there were none: "no men and women then at all." Their grief is offered only as a hypothesis about what might have happened, then handed instead to "mute maternal presences" who do not weep but merely sigh, and whose sighing does not stop the fight so much as maybe, possibly, shake it: the poem's very last line still qualifies itself with "as if." Nothing is confirmed to have ended. The fury is only reported to look like it might be dying.

Muir wrote a poem that refuses anyone, even its own ghosts, the relief of an actual, finished mourning — and then folded it into a book dedicated to a grief he had been carrying, undischarged, for nine years. Set against a man who spent the poem's own gestation stamping ration books and sitting by a hospital bed he could not reach across, that final "as if" starts to look less like a rhetorical flourish and more like the most honest word in the poem: not a resolution, just a poet declining to promise one.
